l: Alcmena, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XV. TO HERACLES THE LION-HEARTED
s: Alcmena bore Heracles in Thebes after Zeus had lain with her.

l: Eurystheus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XV. TO HERACLES THE LION-HEARTED
s: Eurystheus commanded Heracles to wander over unmeasured tracts of land and sea and perform his labors.

l: Olympus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XV. TO HERACLES THE LION-HEARTED
s: Olympus is the glorious home where Heracles now lives happily. It is described as snowy.

l: Heracles' deeds of violence, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XV. TO HERACLES THE LION-HEARTED
s: Heracles performed many deeds of violence while carrying out Eurystheus's bidding. He also endured many hardships during this time.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XVI. TO ASCLEPIUS
s: The unit concerns Asclepius, son of Apollo and healer of sicknesses. Coronis, daughter of King Phlegyas, bore Asclepius in the Dotian plain. Asclepius is described as a great joy to men and a soother of cruel pangs. The speaker offers praise and prayer to Asclepius.

l: Asclepius, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XVI. TO ASCLEPIUS
s: Asclepius is the son of Apollo and a healer of sicknesses. Coronis bore him in the Dotian plain, and he is described as a great joy to men and a soother of cruel pangs. The speaker greets him and offers a prayer in song.

l: Coronis, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XVI. TO ASCLEPIUS
s: Coronis is the daughter of King Phlegyas. She bore Asclepius in the Dotian plain.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XVII. TO THE DIOSCURI
s: The unit concerns Castor and Polydeuces, identified as the Tyndaridae. It says that they sprang from Olympian Zeus and were borne by stately Leda beneath the heights of Taygetus. Zeus had privately bent Leda to his will. The unit hails Castor and Polydeuces as children of Tyndareus and riders upon swift horses.

l: Castor, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XVII. TO THE DIOSCURI
s: Castor is named with Polydeuces as one of the Tyndaridae. He sprang from Olympian Zeus, was borne by Leda beneath the heights of Taygetus, and is hailed as a child of Tyndareus and a rider upon swift horses.

l: Polydeuces, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XVII. TO THE DIOSCURI
s: Polydeuces is named with Castor as one of the Tyndaridae. He sprang from Olympian Zeus, was borne by Leda beneath the heights of Taygetus, and is hailed as a child of Tyndareus and a rider upon swift horses.

l: Dioscuri, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XVII. TO THE DIOSCURI
s: The Tyndaridae are Castor and Polydeuces. They sprang from Olympian Zeus and were borne by Leda beneath the heights of Taygetus.

l: Zeus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XVII. TO THE DIOSCURI
s: Zeus is called Olympian Zeus and the dark-clouded Son of Cronos. He is said to have privately bent Leda to his will, and Castor and Polydeuces sprang from him.

l: Taygetus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XVII. TO THE DIOSCURI
s: Taygetus is associated with the heights beneath which stately Leda bore Castor and Polydeuces.

l: Leda, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XVII. TO THE DIOSCURI
s: Leda is described as stately and as having borne Castor and Polydeuces beneath the heights of Taygetus. The dark-clouded Son of Cronos had privately bent her to his will.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XVIII. TO HERMES
s: The unit praises Hermes, the Cyllenian god and Slayer of Argus, as lord of Cyllene and Arcadia and messenger of the deathless gods. Hermes was born to Maia, the daughter of Atlas, after she joined with Zeus. Maia was a shy goddess who avoided the blessed gods and lived in a shadowy cave, where Zeus visited her at night without the knowledge of gods or mortals. The song ends by greeting Hermes as a giver of grace, guide, and giver of good things.

l: Hermes, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XVIII. TO HERMES
s: Hermes is praised as the Cyllenian god, Slayer of Argus, lord of Cyllene and Arcadia, luck-bringing messenger of the deathless gods. He was born to Maia and Zeus, and is hailed as a giver of grace, guide, and giver of good things.

l: Maia, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XVIII. TO HERMES
s: Maia is the daughter of Atlas and the mother of Hermes. She is described as a shy goddess who avoided the throng of the blessed gods and lived in a shadowy cave, where Zeus visited her at dead of night.

l: Zeus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XVIII. TO HERMES
s: Zeus, the Son of Cronos, lay with Maia at dead of night in her shadowy cave while Hera slept. Neither deathless god nor mortal man knew of this union.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XIX. TO PAN
s: The text praises Pan, the goat-footed, two-horned son of Hermes, as a lively shepherd-god who roams mountains, hunts, and plays his reed pipes with nymphs. It recounts how Hermes fathered Pan with the rich-tressed daughter of Dryops in Arcadia. After Pan’s nurse fled in fear, Hermes carried him to the immortal gods, who welcomed him, while Bacchie Dionysus especially rejoiced. The text ends by greeting Pan and seeking his favor through song.

l: Pan, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XIX. TO PAN
s: Pan is the dear son of Hermes, with goat’s feet, two horns, a full beard, and a love of merry noise. He wanders through wooded glades and mountains, hunts wild beasts, plays sweetly on reed pipes, and dances and sings with the nymphs. The immortals call him Pan because he delights all their hearts.

l: Hermes, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XIX. TO PAN
s: Hermes is Pan’s father and the swift messenger of all the gods. In Arcadia, he tended sheep for a mortal man because he desired to marry the rich-tressed daughter of Dryops, who bore him Pan. Hermes received Pan after the nurse fled, carried him in warm mountain-hare skins to the abodes of the deathless gods, and showed him to them.

l: nymphs, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XIX. TO PAN
s: The nymphs wander and dance with Pan on sheer cliff edges and sing with him beside a spring of dark water. They have clear voices and nimble feet, and they join Pan in songs of the blessed gods, high Olympus, and Hermes.

l: gods, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XIX. TO PAN
s: The gods are presented as the blessed and deathless inhabitants of Olympus. They hear Hermes show them Pan, rejoice at the sight of him, and call him Pan because he delights all their hearts.

l: Arcadia, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XIX. TO PAN
s: Arcadia is described as a land of many springs and the mother of flocks. It contains Hermes’s sacred place as god of Cyllene and is where Hermes tended sheep, desired the daughter of Dryops, and fathered Pan.

l: song, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XIX. TO PAN
s: Song accompanies Pan’s activities, as he plays his reed pipes and sings with the nymphs. The text’s song praises the gods, high Olympus, Hermes, and Pan, and it seeks Pan’s favor.

l: Hymn to Pan, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XIX. TO PAN
s: The Pan hymn praises Pan’s appearance, roaming, hunting, music, dancing, and parentage. It recounts his birth to Hermes and the daughter of Dryops, his reception among the immortals, and the reason for his name. It closes with a greeting to Pan and a promise to remember him in another song.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XX. TO HEPHAESTUS
s: The text praises Hephaestus for his inventions and his role in teaching men glorious gifts. With bright-eyed Athene, Hephaestus taught men crafts that transformed them from cave-dwellers living like wild beasts. After learning these crafts, men lived peacefully in their own houses throughout the year. The speaker asks Hephaestus to grant success and prosperity.

l: Hephaestus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XX. TO HEPHAESTUS
s: Hephaestus is famed for inventions and as a worker. Together with Athene, he taught men glorious gifts and crafts, and the speaker asks him to grant success and prosperity.

l: Athena, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XX. TO HEPHAESTUS
s: Bright-eyed Athene taught men glorious gifts throughout the world together with Hephaestus.

l: men, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XX. TO HEPHAESTUS
s: Before learning crafts, men dwelled in caves in the mountains like wild beasts. After learning crafts through Hephaestus, they lived a peaceful life in their own houses throughout the year.

l: crafts, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XX. TO HEPHAESTUS
s: Men learned crafts through Hephaestus, and these crafts enabled them to live peacefully in their own houses throughout the year.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXI. TO APOLLO
s: The unit praises Apollo, also called Phoebus. A swan sings of him with a clear voice as it lands beside the river Peneus, and a sweet-tongued minstrel sings of him first and last while playing a high-pitched lyre. The speaker greets Apollo as lord and seeks his favor through the song.

l: Apollo, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXI. TO APOLLO
s: Apollo, also called Phoebus, is praised by a swan and by a sweet-tongued minstrel who sings of him first and last while holding a high-pitched lyre. The speaker hails Apollo as lord and seeks his favor with the song.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXII. TO POSEIDON
s: The unit is a hymn to Poseidon, who is described as the great god and mover of the earth and fruitless sea. He is lord of the deep, Helicon, and wide Aegae. The gods allotted him a twofold office as tamer of horses and saviour of ships. The hymn asks Poseidon to be kindly and help those who voyage in ships.

l: Poseidon, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXII. TO POSEIDON
s: Poseidon is described as the great god, mover of the earth and fruitless sea, lord of the deep, Helicon, and wide Aegae. The gods allotted him the twofold office of tamer of horses and saviour of ships. He is called Holder of the Earth and dark-haired lord, and the hymn asks him to be kindly and help those who voyage in ships.

l: sea, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXII. TO POSEIDON
s: The sea is described as fruitless and deep, and Poseidon is its mover and lord.

l: ships, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXII. TO POSEIDON
s: Poseidon is described as a saviour of ships. The hymn asks him to help those who voyage in ships.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXIII. TO THE SON OF CRONOS, MOST HIGH
s: The unit is a hymn to Zeus, the Son of Cronos, most high. Zeus is described as chiefest among the gods, greatest, all-seeing, lord of all, and the fulfiller. He whispers words of wisdom to Themis as she sits leaning toward him. The speaker asks Zeus to be gracious.

l: Zeus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXIII. TO THE SON OF CRONOS, MOST HIGH
s: Zeus is praised as the chiefest and greatest of the gods, all-seeing, lord of all, and the fulfiller. He whispers words of wisdom to Themis as she leans toward him. The speaker asks Zeus to be gracious.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXIV. TO HESTIA
s: The unit addresses Hestia, who tends the holy house of Apollo at goodly Pytho. Hestia is invited to come into the house with one mind with all-wise Zeus. She is also asked to bestow grace on the speaker's song.

l: Hestia, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXIV. TO HESTIA
s: Hestia tends the holy house of Apollo at goodly Pytho. She is invited to come into the house with one mind with all-wise Zeus and to bestow grace on the song.

l: Apollo, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXIV. TO HESTIA
s: Apollo is called the lord and the Far-shooter, and his holy house is at goodly Pytho.

l: house (Apollo's holy house), Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXIV. TO HESTIA
s: The house is Apollo's holy house at goodly Pytho. Hestia tends it, and she is invited to come into it.

s: The song is addressed through a request that Hestia bestow grace on it.

s: The text begins with the Muses, Apollo, and Zeus. The Muses and Apollo are said to bring singers and lyre players into the world, while kings come from Zeus. A person loved by the Muses speaks sweetly, and the Muses and Apollo are asked to honor the speaker’s song.

l: Muses, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXV. TO THE MUSES AND APOLLO
s: The Muses are named at the beginning alongside Apollo and Zeus. Through them, singers appear upon the earth, and those whom they love speak sweetly. They are asked, as children of Zeus, to honor the speaker’s song.

l: Apollo, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXV. TO THE MUSES AND APOLLO
s: Apollo is named with the Muses and Zeus at the beginning. Through Apollo and the Muses, singers and players upon the lyre exist. Apollo is asked to honor the speaker’s song.

l: Zeus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXV. TO THE MUSES AND APOLLO
s: Zeus is named at the beginning and is called the source of kings. The Muses and Apollo are called children of Zeus.

l: singers, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXV. TO THE MUSES AND APOLLO
s: Singers are said to exist upon the earth through the Muses and Apollo.

l: kings, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXV. TO THE MUSES AND APOLLO
s: Kings are said to come from Zeus.

l: song, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXV. TO THE MUSES AND APOLLO
s: The speaker asks the Muses and Apollo to honor the speaker’s song. The speaker says that another song will also be remembered.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXVI. TO DIONYSUS
s: The hymn celebrates Dionysus, the ivy-crowned and loud-crying son of Zeus and Semele. The Nymphs receive, foster, and nurture him in the dells of Nysa, where he grows up in a sweet-smelling cave and is counted among the immortals. Afterward, Dionysus wanders through wooded valleys, followed by the Nymphs, while the forest resounds with their cries. The hymn asks Dionysus to grant that the singers may return rejoicing in future years.

l: Dionysus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXVI. TO DIONYSUS
s: Dionysus is the ivy-crowned, loud-crying son of Zeus and Semele. He grows up in Nysa under the care of the Nymphs, is counted among the immortals, and later wanders through wooded valleys with ivy and laurel, leading the Nymphs.

l: rich-haired Nymphs, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXVI. TO DIONYSUS
s: The Nymphs receive Dionysus from Zeus, foster and nurture him carefully in the dells of Nysa, and bring him up. Later they follow him as their leader through the wooded valleys, filling the forest with their outcry.

l: Nysa, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXVI. TO DIONYSUS
s: Nysa contains the dells and a sweet-smelling cave where Dionysus grows up under the care of the Nymphs.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXVII. TO ARTEMIS
s: The hymn celebrates Artemis as a golden-armed huntress, archer, and pure maiden who delights in pursuing and destroying wild beasts. She hunts across shadowy hills, windy peaks, mountains, woods, and the sea, causing the natural world to tremble and echo. Afterward, she goes to the house of her brother Phoebus Apollo in the rich land of Delphi, where she hangs up her bow and leads the Muses and Graces in dance. The hymn hails Artemis and Apollo as children of Zeus and rich-haired Leto.

l: Artemis, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXVII. TO ARTEMIS
s: Artemis is a golden-armed huntress, archer, and pure maiden who cheers on hounds and shoots stags. She hunts across mountains, woods, and the sea, destroying wild beasts with her arrows; when satisfied, she slackens her bow, goes to Delphi, hangs up her weapons, and leads the dances of the Muses and Graces.

l: Apollo, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXVII. TO ARTEMIS
s: Apollo, also called Phoebus Apollo, is Artemis's brother and has a golden sword. His great house is in the rich land of Delphi, where Artemis goes after hunting.

l: Pytho, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXVII. TO ARTEMIS
s: Delphi is described as a rich land containing the great house of Phoebus Apollo. Artemis goes there after her hunt to hang up her bow and arrows and lead the dances of the Muses and Graces.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXVIII. TO ATHENA
s: The hymn celebrates Pallas Athene, describing her as a bright-eyed, inventive, courageous virgin and saviour of cities. Wise Zeus gives birth to her from his awful head, and she emerges fully armed with a sharp spear. Her appearance causes Olympus to reel, the earth to cry out, and the sea to toss, while the Son of Hyperion stops his horses. Zeus is glad when Athene removes her heavenly armour, and the singer promises to remember her in another song.

l: Pallas Athene, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXVIII. TO ATHENA
s: Pallas Athene is celebrated as a glorious, bright-eyed, inventive, courageous virgin and saviour of cities. She springs fully armed from Zeus’s immortal head, causing Olympus to reel, the earth to cry out, and the sea to toss. She later removes the heavenly armour from her immortal shoulders.

l: Zeus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXVIII. TO ATHENA
s: Zeus bears Pallas Athene from his awful head while she is arrayed in warlike arms. He holds the aegis and is glad after Athene removes her heavenly armour.

l: Olympus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXVIII. TO ATHENA
s: Olympus begins to reel horribly when Pallas Athene emerges from Zeus’s immortal head with her warlike arms and sharp spear.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXIX. TO HESTIA
s: The unit praises Hestia as honored in the dwellings of deathless gods and earth-walking men. It says mortals hold no banquet without pouring sweet wine to Hestia first and last. Hermes is invoked as the slayer of Argus, son of Zeus and Maia, messenger of the blessed gods, bearer of the golden rod, and giver of good. Hestia and Hermes are asked to dwell together in the glorious house and aid the wisdom and strength of men.

l: Hestia, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXIX. TO HESTIA
s: Hestia has an everlasting abode and highest honour in the dwellings of deathless gods and men. Mortals pour sweet wine to her first and last at banquets, and she is asked to dwell together with Hermes and aid the wisdom and strength of men.

l: Hermes, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXIX. TO HESTIA
s: Hermes is identified as the slayer of Argus, son of Zeus and Maia, messenger of the blessed gods, bearer of the golden rod, and giver of good. He is asked, together with Hestia, to dwell in the glorious house and aid the wisdom and strength of men.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXX. TO EARTH THE MOTHER OF ALL
s: The hymn praises Earth as the mother of all and the eldest of all beings. Earth feeds every creature on land, in the sea, and in the air, and gives mortal men the means of life while also taking life away. Men whom Earth honors are blessed in their children and harvests, with abundant crops, livestock, wealth, and orderly cities. The hymn asks Earth, called the mother of the gods and wife of starry Heaven, to grant the singer heart-cheering substance.

l: Earth, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXX. TO EARTH THE MOTHER OF ALL
s: Earth is praised as the well-founded mother of all and the eldest of all beings. She feeds all creatures, blesses men in their children and harvests, gives mortal men the means of life, and can take life away. She is also called the mother of the gods and the wife of starry Heaven.

l: all creatures, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXX. TO EARTH THE MOTHER OF ALL
s: All creatures in the world, including those that walk upon the land, travel the paths of the seas, and fly, are fed from Earth's store.

l: men, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXX. TO EARTH THE MOTHER OF ALL
s: Men are blessed in their children and harvests through Earth. Those whom Earth honors have abundant possessions, fruitful land laden with corn, pastures covered with cattle, houses filled with good things, orderly cities, great riches, and joyful children.

l: harvests, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXX. TO EARTH THE MOTHER OF ALL
s: Harvests are among the blessings Earth grants to men. For men whom Earth honors, the fruitful land is laden with corn.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXXI. TO HELIOS
s: The hymn invokes the Muse Calliope to sing of Helios, the glowing son of Hyperion and Euryphaessa. Helios is described as tireless and godlike, riding a chariot drawn by stallions and shining upon mortals and immortals. He rests at heaven’s highest point after stopping his golden-yoked chariot, then drives his horses down through heaven to Ocean. The speaker greets Helios and asks him to grant heart-cheering substance.

l: Helios, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXXI. TO HELIOS
s: Helios is the tireless, godlike son of Hyperion and Euryphaessa. He rides a golden-yoked chariot drawn by stallions, shines upon mortals and immortals, and gazes piercingly from beneath his golden helmet. After resting at heaven’s highest point, he drives his chariot and horses down through heaven to Ocean.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXXII. TO SELENE
s: The Muses are asked to tell of the long-winged Moon, whose radiant light embraces the earth and makes the air glow. The Moon’s light is brightest at mid-month when her orbit is full, making her a sure token and sign to mortal men. The Son of Cronos joined Selene in love, and she conceived and bore Pandia. Selene is praised as a white-armed, bright, mild goddess and queen.

l: Muses, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXXII. TO SELENE
s: The Muses, daughters of Zeus and well-skilled in song, are asked to tell of the long-winged Moon.

l: Zeus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXXII. TO SELENE
s: Zeus is identified as the father of the Muses.

l: Moon, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXXII. TO SELENE
s: The Moon is long-winged and shines with radiance from heaven, embracing the earth and making the previously unlit air glow. At mid-month her orbit is full and her beams shine brightest, making her a sure token and sign to mortal men.

l: Selene, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXXII. TO SELENE
s: Selene bathes her lovely body in the waters of Ocean, dons her far-gleaming team, and drives her long-maned horses at full speed at eventime in the mid-month. She conceived and bore Pandia after the Son of Cronos joined her in love, and she is hailed as a white-armed, bright, mild, bright-tressed queen.

l: Pandia, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXXII. TO SELENE
s: Pandia is the daughter of Selene and the Son of Cronos. She is described as exceeding lovely among the deathless gods.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXXIII. TO THE DIOSCURI
s: The unit concerns the Tyndaridae, Castor and Polydeuces, whom it calls the glorious children of Leda and Zeus. They are described as deliverers of people on land and of ships caught in stormy seas. When shipmen call upon them, they appear on tawny wings, calm the winds and waves, and bring safety and relief. The song ends by greeting the Tyndaridae and promising to remember them in another song.

l: Dioscuri, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXXIII. TO THE DIOSCURI
s: The Dioscuri are identified with the Tyndaridae, Castor and Polydeuces, the children of Leda and Zeus. They deliver men and ships from storms by appearing on tawny wings, calming the winds, and stilling the waves.

l: Castor, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXXIII. TO THE DIOSCURI
s: Castor is named as one of the Tyndaridae and as a tamer of horses.

l: Polydeuces, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXXIII. TO THE DIOSCURI
s: Polydeuces is named as one of the Tyndaridae and is called blameless.

l: Leda, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXXIII. TO THE DIOSCURI
s: Leda is described as the mother of Castor and Polydeuces. She bore them beneath the peak of Taygetus after lying with Zeus.

l: Zeus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXXIII. TO THE DIOSCURI
s: Zeus is described as the dark-clouded Son of Cronos and as the father of Castor and Polydeuces with Leda.

l: shipmen, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXXIII. TO THE DIOSCURI
s: Shipmen call upon the sons of Zeus when stormy gales threaten their ships. They make vows of white lambs at the forepart of the prow, and they rejoice and find rest when the Dioscuri calm the storm.

l: ships, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXXIII. TO THE DIOSCURI
s: Ships are delivered by Castor and Polydeuces when stormy gales rage over the sea. Their ships may be laid under water by the wind and waves until the two appear and bring relief.

l: sea, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXXIII. TO THE DIOSCURI
s: The sea is described as ruthless and white. Its surface becomes still when the Dioscuri calm the winds and waves.

l: waves, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXXIII. TO THE DIOSCURI
s: The waves of the sea can lay a ship under water during a storm. The Dioscuri still them upon the surface of the sea.

l: deliverance, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XXXIII. TO THE DIOSCURI
s: Deliverance is associated with the Dioscuri, who save men and ships from stormy seas. Their appearance is a fair sign and brings deliverance from toil.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, HOMER’S EPIGRAMS2601
s: The unit presents epigrams concerning hospitality, travel, divine favor, human fortune, and everyday life. Homer appears in a brief exchange with fishermen about what they caught and carried home. Zeus is invoked as father, ruler, protector of strangers, and source of fate and vengeance. Cyme is described as a beautiful high city near Sardene and the Hermus, and as the place from which a disappointed poet wishes to depart.

l: Homer, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, HOMER’S EPIGRAMS2601
s: Homer asks fishermen whether they have caught anything. He responds to their claim that they left behind everything they caught and carried home everything they did not catch by observing that they descend from fathers who possess neither rich lands nor countless sheep.

l: Zeus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, HOMER’S EPIGRAMS2601
s: Zeus is described as the father of the Hermus and as the giver of fate, including the speaker’s unhappy lot from birth. He is said to hold the aegis, to have enabled the people of Phricon to build Aeolian Smyrna, and to send snow in winter. Zeus also rules on high as the god of strangers, whose vengeance follows those who sin against him, and he is called the lord of guests and the guest-table.

l: Cyme, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, HOMER’S EPIGRAMS2601
s: Cyme is called a lovely maiden and a high city near the foothills of Sardene, whose inhabitants drink the water of the divine Hermus. Its people are urged to show reverence to a person who needs a home and a stranger’s support. In another epigram, the speaker says that his limbs do not wish to remain in Cyme’s sacred streets and that he wants to leave for another country.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, FRAGMENTS OF THE EPIC CYCLE / THE WAR OF THE TITANS
s: The Epic Cycle begins with the union of Heaven and Earth, who produce three hundred-handed sons and three Cyclopes. The War of the Titans attributes various traditions to Eumelus, or possibly Arctinus, including descriptions of a shield, Zeus dancing, and the guarded apples of the Hesperides. It also relates that Aegaeon was the son of Earth and Sea and an ally of the Titans. The fragments further connect Cronos with Philyra and Cheiron, and identify the War of the Titans as the earliest source for the story of Heracles sailing in a cauldron.

l: Epic Cycle, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, FRAGMENTS OF THE EPIC CYCLE / THE WAR OF THE TITANS
s: The Epic Cycle begins with the fabled union of Heaven and Earth, from which three hundred-handed sons and three Cyclopes are born.

l: The War of the Titans, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, FRAGMENTS OF THE EPIC CYCLE / THE WAR OF THE TITANS
s: The War of the Titans contains traditions about Heaven, Earth, Aegaeon, the Titans, Zeus, Cronos, Cheiron, Heracles, and the apples of the Hesperides. It is attributed either to Eumelus of Corinth or to Arctinus, and it is identified as the first source for the story of Heracles sailing across the sea in a cauldron.

l: Heaven, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, FRAGMENTS OF THE EPIC CYCLE / THE WAR OF THE TITANS
s: Heaven is said in one account to be the son of Aether. He unites with Earth, and their union produces three hundred-handed sons and three Cyclopes.

l: Earth, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, FRAGMENTS OF THE EPIC CYCLE / THE WAR OF THE TITANS
s: Earth unites with Heaven and bears three hundred-handed sons and three Cyclopes. She is also named as the mother of Aegaeon, together with Sea.

l: Aegaeon, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, FRAGMENTS OF THE EPIC CYCLE / THE WAR OF THE TITANS
s: Aegaeon is said by Eumelus to be the son of Earth and Sea. He dwells in the sea and is an ally of the Titans.

l: Titans, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, FRAGMENTS OF THE EPIC CYCLE / THE WAR OF THE TITANS
s: The Titans have Aegaeon as an ally, according to Eumelus.

l: Eumelus of Corinth, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, FRAGMENTS OF THE EPIC CYCLE / THE WAR OF THE TITANS
s: Eumelus of Corinth is identified as a possible author of the War of the Titans. He says that Aegaeon was the son of Earth and Sea and an ally of the Titans, and he introduces Zeus dancing; the fragments also attribute to him a description of fish on a shield.

l: Zeus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, FRAGMENTS OF THE EPIC CYCLE / THE WAR OF THE TITANS
s: Zeus is introduced by Eumelus as dancing in the midst of others, where he is called the Father of men and gods.

l: Cronos, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, FRAGMENTS OF THE EPIC CYCLE / THE WAR OF THE TITANS
s: Cronos is said by the author of the War of the Giants to have taken the shape of a horse and lain with Philyra, daughter of Ocean. Through this union Cheiron was born a centaur.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE STORY OF OEDIPUS
s: The Story of Oedipus was an epic by Cinaethon consisting of six thousand six hundred verses. Pausanias says it clearly shows that Oedipus’s sons were born to Euryganeia rather than Iocasta. The story also says that the Sphinx killed Haemon, the son of Creon.

l: Story of Oedipus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE STORY OF OEDIPUS
s: The Story of Oedipus was an epic by Cinaethon in six thousand six hundred verses. It says that Oedipus’s sons were born to Euryganeia and that the Sphinx killed Haemon, Creon’s son.

l: Oedipus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE STORY OF OEDIPUS
s: Oedipus is the central figure of the Story of Oedipus. His sons were born to Euryganeia rather than Iocasta, according to the epic.

l: Iocasta, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE STORY OF OEDIPUS
s: Iocasta is said not to have had children by Oedipus in the account cited by Pausanias.

l: Euryganeia, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE STORY OF OEDIPUS
s: Euryganeia was the mother of Oedipus’s sons according to the Story of Oedipus.

l: Haemon, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE STORY OF OEDIPUS
s: Haemon was the dear son of blameless Creon and was described as the comeliest and loveliest of boys. The Sphinx killed him.

l: Sphinx, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE STORY OF OEDIPUS
s: The Sphinx killed Haemon, the son of Creon.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE THEBAID
s: The Thebaid is said to have comprised seven thousand verses and to have begun with a song of parched Argos. It recounts how Polyneices presented Oedipus with treasures of Cadmus, prompting Oedipus to curse his sons and pray that they would never share their inheritance peacefully. It also describes Oedipus cursing his sons after they sent him a haunch, and it tells of Adrastus fleeing Thebes, the burial of seven dead, and the deaths of Parthenopaeus and others in battle.

l: The Thebaid, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE THEBAID
s: The Thebaid was described as an epic of seven thousand verses, beginning with a song of parched Argos. It tells of Oedipus's curses against his sons, Adrastus's flight from Thebes, the burial of seven dead, and the battle in which Parthenopaeus was killed.

l: Polyneices, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE THEBAID
s: Polyneices, described as a heaven-born, golden-haired hero, set beside Oedipus a silver table that had belonged to Cadmus and filled a golden cup with wine. These treasures caused Oedipus great misery and led him to curse his sons.

l: Oedipus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE THEBAID
s: Oedipus became distressed when Polyneices placed before him treasures that had belonged to Cadmus, and he cursed his sons before them. When he saw the haunch they had sent, he threw it to the ground and prayed that each son would fall by the other's hand and go to Hades.

l: the sons of Oedipus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE THEBAID
s: The sons of Oedipus were cursed by their father after Polyneices presented him with Cadmus's treasures and again after they sent him a haunch. Oedipus prayed that they would not divide their father's goods peacefully and that each would die by the other's hand.

l: war and fighting between the sons of Oedipus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE THEBAID
s: Oedipus prayed that war and fighting would always be the portion of his sons rather than their sharing their father's goods in loving brotherhood. He also prayed that each would fall by the hand of the other.

l: Adrastus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE THEBAID
s: Adrastus fled from Thebes wearing miserable garments and took the black-maned Areion with him. After the seven dead received their last rites in Thebes, he lamented the loss of his host, whom he praised as both a good seer and a stout spearman.

l: Thebes, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE THEBAID
s: Thebes was the place from which Adrastus fled in miserable garments. Seven dead received their last rites there, and the battle against the Argives included the death of Parthenopaeus, whose killer was identified differently by the Thebans and by the Thebaid.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE EPIGONI
s: The Epigoni is attributed to Homer and was said to contain seven thousand verses, beginning with an invocation to the Muses about younger men. The Teumesian fox was sent by the gods to punish the descendants of Cadmus, and Cephalus hunted it with his hound after being purified by the Cadmeans for killing Procris. The fox and hound were turned into stones near Teumessus. The Epigoni sent Manto, daughter of Teiresias, to Delphi as a first offering of their spoil, and she later married Rhacius and came to Colophon.

l: Epigoni, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE EPIGONI
s: The Epigoni was attributed to Homer and was said to contain seven thousand verses. It began with the words, “And now, Muses, let us begin to sing of younger men.”

l: Teumesian fox, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE EPIGONI
s: The Teumesian fox was sent by the gods to punish the descendants of Cadmus. The Thebans consequently excluded those of the house of Cadmus from kingship.

l: Cephalus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE EPIGONI
s: Cephalus, son of Deion and an Athenian, owned a hound which no beast could escape. After accidentally killing his wife Procris, he was purified of the homicide by the Cadmeans and hunted the Teumesian fox with his hound.

l: hound, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE EPIGONI
s: Cephalus's hound was said to be able to catch every beast. It overtook the Teumesian fox, and it was then turned into a stone along with the fox near Teumessus.

l: Procris, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE EPIGONI
s: Procris was the wife of Cephalus. Cephalus accidentally killed her and was subsequently purified of the homicide by the Cadmeans.

l: Manto, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE EPIGONI
s: Manto, the daughter of Teiresias, was sent to Delphi by the Epigoni as a first fruit of their spoil. Following an oracle of Apollo, she met and married Rhacius, then came to Colophon and wept over the destruction of her country.

l: Epigoni (the victorious descendants), Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE EPIGONI
s: The Epigoni sent Manto to Delphi as a first fruit of their spoil. An oracle of Apollo directed her to marry the man she met, who was Rhacius.

l: Rhacius, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE EPIGONI
s: Rhacius was the son of Lebes and a Mycenaean by race. He met and married Manto in accordance with Apollo's oracle.

l: Colophon, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE EPIGONI
s: Manto came to Colophon after marrying Rhacius. There she was much cast down and wept over the destruction of her country.

l: hunting of the Teumesian fox, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE EPIGONI
s: Cephalus hunted the Teumesian fox with his hound after the Cadmeans purified him for killing Procris. The hound and fox overtook one another and were then turned into stones near Teumessus.

l: transformation of the hound and fox into stones, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE EPIGONI
s: After the hound had overtaken the Teumesian fox, both animals were turned into stones near Teumessus.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE CYPRIA
s: The Cypria recounts Zeus and Themis’s plan to bring about the Trojan war, beginning with the dispute among Hera, Athena, and Aphrodite over their beauty and Alexandrus’s judgment in favor of Aphrodite. It describes Alexandrus’s abduction of Helen from Sparta, the preparations and early campaigns of the Greek expedition against Ilium, and the first battles and losses at Troy. The poem also relates events involving Castor and Polydeuces, Odysseus and Palamedes, the sacrifice of Iphigeneia, Achilles’s actions, and the deaths of Protesilaus and Palamedes. Its fragments additionally preserve traditions about the marriage of Peleus and Thetis, Helen’s birth, and various heroes and gods.

l: The Cypria, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE CYPRIA
s: The Cypria is an epic said to have been current in eleven books, continuing the account of the Trojan war. It recounts events from Zeus’s plan with Themis through the early Greek campaign against Troy, and fragments attribute various genealogical, mythological, and narrative details to its poet.

l: Zeus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE CYPRIA
s: Zeus plans with Themis to bring about the Trojan war in order to relieve the earth of its burden of men. He sends Hermes to lead Hera, Athena, and Aphrodite to Alexandrus for judgment, and he gives Polydeuces immortality every other day after Castor’s death.

l: Trojan War, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE CYPRIA
s: The Trojan war is brought about through Zeus’s plan to relieve the earth of its excessive human population. Its causes include the dispute among Hera, Athena, and Aphrodite and Alexandrus’s choice of Aphrodite.

l: Strife, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE CYPRIA
s: Strife arrives while the gods are feasting at the marriage of Peleus and Thetis and starts the dispute over which of Hera, Athena, and Aphrodite is fairest.

l: Hera, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE CYPRIA
s: Hera competes with Athena and Aphrodite for the judgment of Alexandrus. She later stirs up a storm against Alexandrus and Helen while they are sailing from Sparta.

l: Athena, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE CYPRIA
s: Athena is one of the three goddesses judged by Alexandrus as the fairest. At the marriage of Peleus and Thetis, she polishes the ashen spear shaft given to Peleus by Cheiron.

l: Aphrodite, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE CYPRIA
s: Aphrodite wins Alexandrus’s judgment by promising him marriage with Helen. She advises him to build ships, brings Helen and Alexandrus together, arranges their meeting with Helen, and is described as wearing flowered garments and garlands.

l: Alexandrus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE CYPRIA
s: Alexandrus judges Aphrodite fairest after she promises him marriage with Helen. He builds ships, sails to Sparta, gives gifts to Helen, carries her and great treasures away by night, takes Sidon, and returns to Troy to celebrate his marriage with her.

l: Helen, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE CYPRIA
s: Helen is promised to Alexandrus by Aphrodite and is brought together with him while Menelaus is away in Crete. She leaves Sparta with Alexandrus and arrives at Ilium in three days according to the Cypria; she is also said to have been born to Nemesis after Zeus pursued her.

l: Sparta, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE CYPRIA
s: Sparta is where Menelaus entertains Alexandrus and where Alexandrus gives gifts to Helen. Helen later leaves Sparta with Alexandrus while Menelaus is away.

l: Menelaus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE CYPRIA
s: Menelaus entertains Alexandrus in Sparta but then sails for Crete, leaving Helen to provide for the guests. After Iris tells him what has happened, he returns, plans an expedition against Ilium with his brother, and visits Nestor.

l: Troy, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE CYPRIA
s: Troy is the destination of Alexandrus and Helen after their flight from Sparta, where they celebrate their marriage. The Greek forces later attack Troy, lay waste to surrounding territories, and fight its defenders.

l: Ilium, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE CYPRIA
s: Ilium is the city against which Menelaus and his allies plan an expedition. The Greeks attempt to land there, are initially prevented by the Trojans, and later demand that the city surrender Helen and the treasure taken with her.

l: Castor, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE CYPRIA
s: Castor is caught stealing cattle with Polydeuces from Idas and Lynceus and is killed by Idas. He is mortal, while Polydeuces is immortal, and Zeus grants the two brothers immortality on alternate days.

l: Polydeuces, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE CYPRIA
s: Polydeuces takes part with Castor in stealing the cattle of Idas and Lynceus. After Castor is killed, Polydeuces kills Lynceus and Idas, and Zeus grants him and Castor immortality every other day.

l: Greek expedition against Ilium, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE CYPRIA
s: The Greek expedition against Ilium is planned by Menelaus and his brother and assembled by gathering leaders across Hellas. It musters at Aulis, mistakenly sacks Teuthrania, is scattered by a storm, reforms, and eventually sails toward Ilium.

l: Odysseus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE CYPRIA
s: Odysseus initially pretends to be mad because he does not wish to join the expedition. The leaders detect his deception when Palamedes suggests seizing Odysseus’s son Telemachus for punishment.

l: Palamedes, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE CYPRIA
s: Palamedes suggests seizing Telemachus to expose Odysseus’s feigned madness. According to the Cypria, Diomedes and Odysseus cause Palamedes’s death by drowning him while he is out fishing.

l: Achaeans, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE CYPRIA
s: The Achaeans assemble at Aulis, sacrifice, and witness the serpent and sparrows incident before Calchas gives his prophecy. They later attack Ilium, demand Helen and her treasure, and lay waste to surrounding cities.

l: Greeks, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE CYPRIA
s: The Greeks gather for the expedition against Ilium and are initially scattered by a storm after attacking Teuthrania. At Tenedos, they leave Philoctetes behind in Lemnos, and at Ilium they lose Protesilaus before Achilles drives the Trojans back.

l: Aulis, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE CYPRIA
s: Aulis is where the Greek leaders first meet and sacrifice before the expedition. The forces later muster there a second time, but stormy winds sent by Artemis prevent them from sailing.

l: Achilles, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE CYPRIA
s: Achilles wounds Telephus, marries Deidameia at Scyros, and later helps heal Telephus so he can guide the Greeks to Ilium. He kills Cycnus, drives back the Trojans, sacks several cities, kills Troilus, receives Briseis as a prize, and restrains the Achaeans from returning home.

l: Agamemnon, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE CYPRIA
s: Agamemnon provides the feast for the leaders and is involved in organizing the expedition. After killing a stag and boasting that he surpassed Artemis, he causes her anger and the demand that Iphigeneia be sacrificed.

l: Artemis, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE CYPRIA
s: Artemis becomes angry when Agamemnon kills a stag and boasts that he surpasses her, sending stormy winds that prevent the Greeks from sailing. When Iphigeneia is brought for sacrifice, Artemis snatches her away, transports her to the Tauri, makes her immortal, and puts a stag in her place.

l: Iphigeneia, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE CYPRIA
s: Iphigeneia is summoned to Aulis under the pretense that she will marry Achilles so that she can be sacrificed to Artemis. Artemis rescues her, transports her to the Tauri, and makes her immortal.

l: Hector, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE CYPRIA
s: Hector kills Protesilaus when the Greeks attempt to land at Ilium.

l: Briseis, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE CYPRIA
s: Briseis is taken among the spoils of the cities attacked by Achilles and is awarded to him as a prize.

l: Chryseis, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE CYPRIA
s: Chryseis is taken among the spoils, and Agamemnon receives her as a prize. The Cypria is said to state that she had taken refuge at, or gone to, Hypoplacian Thebes to sacrifice to Artemis.

l: Patroclus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE CYPRIA
s: Patroclus carries Lycaon away to Lemnos and sells him as a slave.

l: marriage of Peleus and Thetis, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE CYPRIA
s: At the marriage of Peleus and Thetis, the gods gather on Mount Pelion to feast and bring gifts for Peleus. Cheiron gives Peleus an ashen spear shaft, Athena polishes it, and Hephaestus fits it with a head; Strife’s arrival at the feast begins the dispute among Hera, Athena, and Aphrodite.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE AETHIOPIS
s: The Aethiopis, attributed to Arctinus of Miletus, follows the Iliad and concerns the final events of the Trojan War. Penthesileia comes to aid the Trojans but is killed by Achilles, who is later purified after killing Thersites. Memnon kills Antilochus and is then killed by Achilles, while Achilles is subsequently killed by Paris and Apollo. The Achaeans recover and bury Achilles, and a dispute over his arms arises between Odysseus and Aias, who later kills himself.

l: The Aethiopis, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE AETHIOPIS
s: The Aethiopis is a five-book work by Arctinus of Miletus that follows the Iliad. It recounts the arrivals of Penthesileia and Memnon, the deaths of Antilochus, Memnon, and Achilles, the burial of Achilles, and the dispute over his arms.

l: Iliad, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE AETHIOPIS
s: The Iliad follows the Cypria and is followed by the five books of the Aethiopis.

l: Penthesileia, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE AETHIOPIS
s: Penthesileia, the daughter of Ares and of Thracian race, comes to aid the Trojans. She shows great prowess but is killed by Achilles, and the Trojans bury her.

l: Trojans, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE AETHIOPIS
s: The Trojans receive Penthesileia as an ally and bury her after Achilles kills her. They also receive aid from Memnon, and later struggle to recover Achilles's body before Aias and Odysseus drive them back.

l: Achilles, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE AETHIOPIS
s: Achilles kills Penthesileia and later kills Memnon after Memnon slays Antilochus. He kills Thersites for abusing and reviling him, is purified by Odysseus, and is eventually killed by Paris and Apollo.

l: Achaeans, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE AETHIOPIS
s: The Achaeans dispute Achilles's killing of Thersites. They bury Antilochus, lay out Achilles's body, pile a cairn for him, hold games in his honour, and later dispute the possession of his arms.

l: Odysseus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE AETHIOPIS
s: Odysseus purifies Achilles after the killing of Thersites. During the struggle for Achilles's body, he drives off the Trojans behind Aias.

l: Memnon, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE AETHIOPIS
s: Memnon, the son of Eos, comes to aid the Trojans wearing armour made by Hephaestus. He kills Antilochus but is then killed by Achilles, after which Eos obtains immortality for him from Zeus.

l: Thetis, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE AETHIOPIS
s: Thetis tells Achilles about Memnon. After Achilles dies, she arrives with the Muses and her sisters to bewail him, then takes him from the pyre and transports him to the White Island.

l: Antilochus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE AETHIOPIS
s: Antilochus is slain by Memnon. The Achaeans bury him.

l: Paris, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE AETHIOPIS
s: Paris kills Achilles together with Apollo.

l: Aias, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE AETHIOPIS
s: Aias takes up Achilles's body and carries it to the ships while Odysseus drives off the Trojans. He later disputes with Odysseus over Achilles's arms and kills himself about dawn.

l: the body of Achilles, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE AETHIOPIS
s: After Achilles is killed, Aias carries his body to the ships while Odysseus drives off the Trojans. The Achaeans lay it out, and Thetis later takes it from the pyre and transports it to the White Island.

l: Achilles’ arms, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE AETHIOPIS
s: The arms of Achilles become the subject of a dispute between Odysseus and Aias.

l: the arrival of Penthesileia, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE AETHIOPIS
s: Penthesileia arrives to aid the Trojans and demonstrates great prowess before Achilles kills her.

l: the killing of Penthesileia, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE AETHIOPIS
s: Achilles kills Penthesileia after she comes to aid the Trojans. The Trojans bury her, and Achilles is later criticized by Thersites for what is described as his supposed love for her.

l: the battle between the Achaeans and Trojans, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE AETHIOPIS
s: The Achaeans and Trojans fight after Memnon arrives to aid Troy. During the fighting, Memnon kills Antilochus, Achilles kills Memnon, and Achilles later routs the Trojans.

l: the death of Antilochus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE AETHIOPIS
s: Antilochus is killed by Memnon. The Achaeans bury him afterward.

l: the death of Memnon, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE AETHIOPIS
s: Memnon is killed by Achilles after killing Antilochus. Eos then obtains immortality for Memnon from Zeus.

l: the death of Achilles, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE AETHIOPIS
s: Achilles is killed by Paris and Apollo after routing the Trojans and rushing into the city with them.

l: the struggle for Achilles's body, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE AETHIOPIS
s: A great struggle takes place over Achilles's body after his death. Aias carries the body to the ships, while Odysseus drives off the Trojans.

l: the funeral of Achilles, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE AETHIOPIS
s: The Achaeans lay out Achilles's body, while Thetis and the Muses bewail him. Thetis takes him from the pyre and transports him to the White Island; the Achaeans then pile a cairn and hold games in his honour.

l: the dispute between Odysseus and Aias, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE AETHIOPIS
s: A dispute arises between Odysseus and Aias over the arms of Achilles.

l: Aias’s suicide, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE AETHIOPIS
s: Aias kills himself about dawn.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE LITTLE ILIAD
s: The Little Iliad, attributed to Lesches of Mitylene, recounts events after Achilles’ death leading to the fall of Troy. Odysseus wins Achilles’ arms through Athena’s contriving, captures Helenus, helps bring Philoctetes and Neoptolemus to the war, and steals the Palladium with Diomedes. Philoctetes kills Alexandrus, Neoptolemus kills Eurypylus, and Epeius builds the wooden horse, which the Trojans bring into Ilium after the Achaeans sail to Tenedos. The fragments also describe the night sack of Ilium, including the deaths of Priam and Astyanax and the enslavement of Andromache.

l: The Little Iliad, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE LITTLE ILIAD
s: The Little Iliad is a four-book epic by Lesches of Mitylene. It describes the adjudging of Achilles’ arms, the bringing of Philoctetes and Neoptolemus to Troy, the construction of the wooden horse, and events during the sack of Ilium.

l: Lesches of Pyrrha or Mitylene, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE LITTLE ILIAD
s: Lesches of Mitylene is identified as the author of the four-book Little Iliad. The fragments also attribute to him accounts of the quarrel between Aias and Odysseus, Odysseus’s disguise, and details of the fall of Ilium.

l: Achaeans, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE LITTLE ILIAD
s: The Achaeans adjudge Achilles’ arms, besiege the Trojans, place their best men in the wooden horse, burn their huts, and sail to Tenedos. During the sack, they kill or capture many inhabitants of Ilium.

l: Achilles, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE LITTLE ILIAD
s: Achilles’ arms are awarded after his death, and his ghost appears to Neoptolemus. A storm also carries Achilles to Scyros in an account preserved from the Little Iliad.

l: Achilles’ arms, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE LITTLE ILIAD
s: Achilles’ arms are awarded to Odysseus through Athena’s contriving. Odysseus later gives them to Neoptolemus.

l: Odysseus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE LITTLE ILIAD
s: Odysseus wins Achilles’ arms, lies in wait for and captures Helenus, and helps bring Neoptolemus from Scyros. He disguises himself as a beggar to enter Ilium, plots with Helen, kills some Trojans, steals the Palladium with Diomedes, and recognizes Helicaon during the night battle.

l: Athena, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE LITTLE ILIAD
s: Athena contrives for Odysseus to gain Achilles’ arms and gives Epeius instructions for building the wooden horse. She is also invoked in the account of the girls’ argument favoring Odysseus over Aias.

l: Aias, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE LITTLE ILIAD
s: Aias quarrels with Odysseus over their achievements and is said to have carried Achilles’ body from the fighting. After Odysseus receives Achilles’ arms, Aias goes mad, destroys the Achaeans’ herd, and kills himself; he is buried in a coffin because of the king’s anger.

l: Helenus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE LITTLE ILIAD
s: Helenus is captured by Odysseus. He prophesies what is required for the taking of Troy, leading to Diomedes’ bringing Philoctetes from Lemnos.

l: Diomedes, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE LITTLE ILIAD
s: Diomedes brings Philoctetes from Lemnos after Helenus prophesies about the taking of Troy. He also helps Odysseus carry the Palladium out of Troy.

l: Philoctetes, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE LITTLE ILIAD
s: Philoctetes is brought from Lemnos by Diomedes and healed by Machaon. He fights Alexandrus in single combat and kills him, and he later kills Admetus according to a fragment.

l: Helen, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE LITTLE ILIAD
s: Helen recognizes Odysseus when he enters Ilium disguised as a beggar and plots with him for the city’s capture. She marries Deiphobus after Alexandrus’s death and later consents to the release of Aethra.

l: Neoptolemus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE LITTLE ILIAD
s: Neoptolemus is brought from Scyros by Odysseus and receives Achilles’ arms; Achilles’ ghost appears to him. He kills Eurypylus, Eion, Agenor, Astynous, and Priam, and takes Andromache as his prize after throwing Astyanax from a tower.

l: Eurypylus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE LITTLE ILIAD
s: Eurypylus son of Telephus arrives to aid the Trojans, displays his prowess, and is killed by Neoptolemus. Another fragment says that Eurypylus killed Machaon.

l: Troy, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE LITTLE ILIAD
s: Troy is the city whose capture is prophesied by Helenus. Its inhabitants recover and bury Alexandrus, destroy part of their wall, bring the wooden horse inside, and celebrate as though they had defeated the Achaeans.

l: Ilium, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE LITTLE ILIAD
s: Ilium is entered by Odysseus in disguise and later captured after the Trojans bring in the wooden horse. During the sack, Priam is killed at the doors of his house, Astyanax is thrown from a tower, and Andromache is taken by Neoptolemus.

l: Epeius, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE LITTLE ILIAD
s: Epeius builds the wooden horse by Athena’s instruction.

l: wooden horse, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE LITTLE ILIAD
s: The wooden horse contains the Achaeans’ best men. After the Achaean forces sail to Tenedos, the Trojans bring the horse into their city and feast as if their troubles were over.

l: Menelaus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE LITTLE ILIAD
s: Menelaus outrages Alexandrus’s dead body, though the Trojans recover and bury it. He is also said to cast away his sword when he sees Helen’s unclad breasts.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE SACK OF ILIUM
s: The Sack of Ilium, attributed to Arctinus of Miletus, describes the Greek capture and destruction of Ilium through the wooden horse. The Trojans debate what to do with the horse, but dedicate it to Athena before Sinon signals the Achaeans, who enter the city and storm it. Priam, Polyxena, Astyanax, and others die, while Helen, Andromache, Aethra, and the spoils are taken by the Greeks. After burning Ilium, the Greeks sail away, and Athena plans to destroy them at sea.

l: The Sack of Ilium, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE SACK OF ILIUM
s: The Sack of Ilium is described as a two-book work by Arctinus of Miletus. It recounts the capture, sack, and burning of Ilium, the division of spoils, and the Greeks' departure.

l: Ilium, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE SACK OF ILIUM
s: Ilium is captured and stormed by the Greeks after Sinon raises a fire-signal and the warriors hidden in the wooden horse emerge. The city is burned, and its inhabitants and treasures are divided among the Greeks.

l: Arctinus of Miletus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE SACK OF ILIUM
s: Arctinus of Miletus is identified as the author of the Sack of Ilium. His account includes the fall of Ilium, the deaths and captures that follow it, and details about the Palladium and the physicians Machaon and Podaleirius.

l: Trojans, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE SACK OF ILIUM
s: The Trojans suspect the wooden horse and debate whether to throw it from the rocks, burn it, or dedicate it to Athena. They choose to dedicate it and then feast, believing the war has ended, before the Greeks attack.

l: wooden horse, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE SACK OF ILIUM
s: The Trojans debate what should be done with the wooden horse and finally dedicate it to Athena. Greek warriors hidden inside it later come out and attack the Trojans.

l: Athena, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE SACK OF ILIUM
s: The Trojans dedicate the wooden horse to Athena. Aias the son of Ileus tears away her image with Cassandra, and he later takes refuge at her altar; after the Greeks depart, Athena plans to destroy them on the high seas.

l: Trojan War, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE SACK OF ILIUM
s: The Trojans believe the war is over when they dedicate the wooden horse to Athena and begin feasting. The Greeks then attack and sack Ilium.

l: Sinon, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE SACK OF ILIUM
s: Sinon raises the fire-signal to the Achaeans after getting into Ilium by pretence. His signal helps bring the Greek ships from Tenedos and begins the attack.

l: Achaeans, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE SACK OF ILIUM
s: The Achaeans sail from Tenedos after Sinon raises the fire-signal. They emerge from the wooden horse or join those who emerge, kill many Trojans, storm Ilium, divide the spoils, and later sail away.

l: storming of Ilium, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE SACK OF ILIUM
s: The storming of Ilium begins when the Greeks hidden in the wooden horse come out and the Achaeans arrive from Tenedos. Many enemies are killed, and the city is captured.

l: Neoptolemus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE SACK OF ILIUM
s: Neoptolemus kills Priam, who has fled to the altar of Zeus Herceius. He takes Andromache as his prize.

l: Priam, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE SACK OF ILIUM
s: Priam flees to the altar of Zeus Herceius during the sack of Ilium. Neoptolemus kills him there.

l: Menelaus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE SACK OF ILIUM
s: Menelaus finds Helen and takes her to the ships. He also kills Deiphobus.

l: Helen, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE SACK OF ILIUM
s: Helen is found by Menelaus during the sack of Ilium. Menelaus takes her to the ships.

l: Aias the son of Ileus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE SACK OF ILIUM
s: Aias the son of Ileus tries to drag Cassandra away by force and tears away the image of Athena with her. The Greeks decide to stone him, but he escapes by taking refuge at Athena's altar.

l: Cassandra, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE SACK OF ILIUM
s: Aias the son of Ileus tries to drag Cassandra away by force. In doing so, he tears away the image of Athena with her.

l: burning of Ilium, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE SACK OF ILIUM
s: The Greeks burn Ilium after storming and capturing the city.

l: Polyxena, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE SACK OF ILIUM
s: The Greeks sacrifice Polyxena at the tomb of Achilles after burning Ilium.

l: Achilles, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE SACK OF ILIUM
s: Polyxena is sacrificed at Achilles' tomb after the Greeks capture and burn Ilium.

l: Odysseus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE SACK OF ILIUM
s: Odysseus murders Astyanax during the sack of Ilium.

l: Astyanax, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE SACK OF ILIUM
s: Odysseus murders Astyanax. A scholiast also reports that the author of the Sack says Astyanax was hurled from the city wall.

l: Andromache, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE SACK OF ILIUM
s: Neoptolemus takes Andromache as his prize after the Greeks sack Ilium.

l: departure of the Greeks, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE SACK OF ILIUM
s: After burning Ilium, sacrificing Polyxena, taking captives, and dividing the spoils, the Greeks sail away. Athena plans to destroy them on the high seas.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE RETURNS
s: The Returns by Agias of Troezen describes the Greek leaders’ journeys after the Sack of Ilium, including quarrels, storms, deaths, burials, and homecomings. Athena causes a quarrel between Agamemnon and Menelaus, while Achilles’ ghost warns Agamemnon and his followers of what will happen. Neoptolemus travels overland, meets Odysseus, buries Phoenix, and is recognized by Peleus. The poem also recounts Agamemnon’s murder by Aegisthus and Clytaemnestra, Orestes and Pylades’ vengeance, and Menelaus’s return home.

l: Returns, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE RETURNS
s: The Returns, attributed to Agias of Troezen, follows the Sack of Ilium and recounts the Greeks’ journeys home. It includes the quarrel between Agamemnon and Menelaus, the storm at the Capherides, Neoptolemus’s overland journey, Agamemnon’s murder, Orestes and Pylades’ vengeance, and Menelaus’s return. It also contains accounts of Hades and its terrors, Medea’s rejuvenation of Aeson, Antiope’s betrayal of Themiscyra, and Tantalus’s punishment.

l: The Sack of Ilium, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE RETURNS
s: The Sack of Ilium precedes the events narrated in The Returns.

l: Athena, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE RETURNS
s: Athena causes a quarrel between Agamemnon and Menelaus about the voyage from Troy. Agamemnon stays behind to appease her anger.

l: Agamemnon, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE RETURNS
s: Agamemnon quarrels with Menelaus after the voyage from Troy, and he remains behind to appease Athena’s anger. When he later sails away, Achilles’ ghost appears and tries to prevent him by foretelling what will befall him. Agamemnon is later murdered by Aegisthus and Clytaemnestra.

l: Menelaus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE RETURNS
s: Menelaus quarrels with Agamemnon about the voyage from Troy. He later sails with five ships, reaches Egypt after the rest are destroyed on the high seas, and eventually returns home.

l: Achilles, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE RETURNS
s: Achilles appears as a ghost when Agamemnon and his followers are sailing away. He tries to prevent them from continuing by foretelling what will befall them.

l: Neoptolemus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE RETURNS
s: Warned by Thetis, Neoptolemus travels overland and meets Odysseus at Maronea in Thrace. He buries Phoenix after Phoenix dies on the journey and is recognized by Peleus when he reaches the Molossi.

l: Odysseus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE RETURNS
s: Odysseus meets Neoptolemus at Maronea in Thrace.

l: Aegisthus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE RETURNS
s: Aegisthus murders Agamemnon together with Clytaemnestra.

l: Clytaemnestra, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE RETURNS
s: Clytaemnestra murders Agamemnon together with Aegisthus.

l: Orestes, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE RETURNS
s: Orestes takes vengeance for Agamemnon’s murder together with Pylades.

l: Agamemnon's murder, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE RETURNS
s: Agamemnon’s murder is committed by Aegisthus and Clytaemnestra. Orestes and Pylades subsequently take vengeance for it.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE TELEGONY
s: The Telegony tells of Odysseus’s travels after the Odyssey, including his visit to Elis, sacrifices in Ithaca, marriage to Callidice in Thesprotis, and war against the Brygi. After Callidice’s death, Odysseus returns to Ithaca, where Telegonus arrives and ravages the island. Odysseus comes out to defend Ithaca but is unwittingly killed by Telegonus, who then takes his body, Penelope, and Telemachus to his mother’s island. Circe makes them immortal, after which Telegonus marries Penelope and Telemachus marries Circe.

l: The Telegony, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE TELEGONY
s: The Telegony is a poem in two books by Eugammon of Cyrene. It concerns the events following the Returns and the Odyssey, including Odysseus’s travels, his death at the hands of Telegonus, and the immortality granted by Circe.

l: Penelope, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE TELEGONY
s: Penelope is transported with Odysseus’s body and Telemachus to Telegonus’s mother’s island. Circe makes her immortal, and Telegonus marries her.

l: Odysseus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE TELEGONY
s: Odysseus sacrifices to the Nymphs, visits Elis, returns to Ithaca, performs the sacrifices ordered by Teiresias, and goes to Thesprotis. He leads the Thesprotians against the Brygi, marries Callidice, later returns to Ithaca, and is unwittingly killed by Telegonus while defending the island.

l: Ithaca, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE TELEGONY
s: Odysseus returns to Ithaca after Callidice’s death. Telegonus later lands there and ravages the island, prompting Odysseus to defend it.

l: Thesprotis, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE TELEGONY
s: Thesprotis is where Odysseus goes after performing the sacrifices ordered by Teiresias. Its queen, Callidice, marries Odysseus, and its forces are led by Odysseus in a war against the Brygi.

l: Callidice, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE TELEGONY
s: Callidice is queen of the Thesprotians and marries Odysseus. After her death, Polypoetes, the son of Odysseus, succeeds to the kingdom, while Odysseus returns to Ithaca.

l: Telegonus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE TELEGONY
s: Telegonus is the son Odysseus has by Calypso. While searching for his father, he lands on Ithaca and ravages it, then unwittingly kills Odysseus; after learning his mistake, he transports Odysseus’s body, Penelope, and Telemachus to his mother’s island and later marries Penelope.

l: killing of Odysseus by Telegonus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE TELEGONY
s: Telegonus kills Odysseus unwittingly when Odysseus comes out to defend Ithaca from the ravaging of the island. Telegonus learns his mistake afterward and transports Odysseus’s body to his mother’s island.

l: mother's island, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE TELEGONY
s: Telegonus transports Odysseus’s body, Penelope, and Telemachus to his mother’s island. Circe makes them immortal there.

l: Circe, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE TELEGONY
s: Circe makes Odysseus, Penelope, and Telemachus immortal on her island. Telemachus marries her.

l: Telemachus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE TELEGONY
s: Telemachus is identified as a son of Odysseus. Telegonus transports him with Odysseus’s body and Penelope to his mother’s island, where Circe makes him immortal; he then marries Circe.
